rationale: Inbox intake of the founder's Deep Memory home page, flagged by the intake as NEW TO THE LEDGER AND SUPPLIED BY ITS AUTHOR. I propose it as one Source record (a self-published, AI-assisted web essay by the founder, carrying the recorded permission line verbatim) and catalogue its distinct testable propositions as claims anchored to that source by [§ …] section and verbatim quote — unfeatured, ungraded, for the editions to weigh. Because the source is the founder's own essay, evidence records on it are weak `supports`, `qualifies` or `context`, with limitations saying so. Every one of the 25 works the page names came back with no OpenAlex result and no retrieved text is in `sources`, so each is dispositioned `blocked` with the route to its primary; nothing is quoted from any of them. No corrections (the ledger holds no records to correct). No edition candidate: the record deepens without the telling changing, though the article's line that no founding page has yet entered will need refreshing once this source is admitted.

A self-published web essay by the case's founder, not peer-reviewed; the page states 'AI assists the research; its output is not a substitute for the evidence.'

Founder-supplied hypothesis material: its propositions enter the catalog as claims to be tested; its statements about objects, dates and statistics are secondary reports (many sourced by the page to Wikipedia/Commons and to the site's own unaudited experiments) and count as context or weak support at most.
Text read: the pipeline's tag-stripped extraction of the HTML, with [§ …] headings kept as section markers; the HTML beside it is the original.

evidence.title: Deep Memory home page: the visual grammar people notice across distant objects
evidence.sourceStatement: The page's opening narrative states that, set side by side, a bird-headed figure, a handled shape and hands on a stone body from distant places look alike: "distant objects can share a surprisingly familiar visual grammar". It then states that a resemblance is only a starting observation whose meaning depends on dates, contexts, differences and connections.
evidence.editorInference: Editor: this is the founder's framing of the phenomenon, not an independent observation of the objects; it establishes what the case is about and carries no diagnostic weight for or against any explanation.
limitations: Self-published, AI-assisted essay by the founder.
States the impression, not a measured comparison.

evidence.title: Deep Memory reports its catalogue experiment's bird-person frequency
evidence.sourceStatement: The page reports that its catalogue experiment "finds its broad bird-person class in 55% of the 926 sampled traditions", adding that this gives a baseline for the category but does not tell how often a particular pose, object and arrangement occur together.
evidence.editorInference: Editor: a self-report of the site's own unaudited experiment; the figure supports the claim only as the page's statement of its result. The underlying catalogue (Berezkin & Duvakin) and the site's method page are not in hand.
limitations: Self-report of the author's own experiment; method and data not retrieved.
The page itself notes the 2016 catalogue has uneven coverage.

evidence.title: Deep Memory reports its catalogue experiment's cosmic-serpent frequency
evidence.sourceStatement: The page states that the catalogue analysis "reports a broad cosmic-serpent class in 37% of its sampled traditions" and that this result describes the selected category and dataset only.
evidence.editorInference: Editor: same footing as EV-DEEP-002 — the site's own result, reported by its author.
limitations: Self-report of the author's own experiment; method and data not retrieved.

evidence.title: Deep Memory's stated caution on catalogue coverage
evidence.sourceStatement: In the limitations of study 02 the page states: "The 2016 catalogue has uneven coverage, particularly for the ancient Near East" and Rapa Nui, and that broad narrative categories are not the specific images or place names in the claim.
evidence.editorInference: Editor: the author's own qualification of the frequency figures; it narrows how far the 55% and 37% baselines reach without denying them.
limitations: Author's own limitation statement; the catalogue's coverage has not been independently checked.

evidence.title: Deep Memory reports the V1 civiliser lineup result
evidence.sourceStatement: The page states that in the V1 experiment "claimed partners ranked first in 62.5% of completed lineups", versus 9% for random pairs, and that the V2 source audit inspected 29 passages without rerunning the similarity test.
evidence.editorInference: Editor: self-report of the site's AI lineup experiment; the number is the page's statement of its own result.
limitations: 'Completed lineups' implies incomplete runs the page does not enumerate here.

evidence.title: Deep Memory's stated limits on the V1 lineups
evidence.sourceStatement: The page's limitations for study 04 state: "The lineups were recognisable and used compressed modern accounts." It adds that neither V1 nor the V2 audit establishes a worldwide rarity rate or a shared origin.
evidence.editorInference: Editor: the author's own qualification — recognisable lineups and compressed modern retellings mean the 62.5% figure may measure familiarity with a composite biography rather than similarity between original accounts.

evidence.title: Deep Memory reports the flood text-coding pilot's pattern
evidence.sourceStatement: The page states that the "coded summaries show regional clustering and an uneven distribution" of details associated with Genesis, alongside widespread generic flood motifs, and that the experiment maps details in 263 summaries.
evidence.editorInference: Editor: self-report of an AI coding of a compiler's summaries (the page's own limitation); supports the claims only as the page's statement of its result.
limitations: Self-report; the page notes one AI coded a compiler's summaries, not original accounts.

evidence.title: Deep Memory reports what the image pilots exposed
evidence.sourceStatement: The page states the three image pilots exposed "altered illustrations, unreliable feature coding and strong disagreement between judges" and that "Matching the kinds of objects changed the lineup result."
evidence.editorInference: Editor: self-report of the site's pilots; these are negative or cautionary findings about method rather than about the objects.
limitations: The page notes incomplete runs and cropping constrain the conclusions.

evidence.title: Deep Memory's caption on the Jiroft handbag's wear
evidence.sourceStatement: The caption for the Jiroft chlorite 'handbag' states it is "Worn on the handle as if hung on a cord." The page points to the Halil Rud wear study (Vidale & Micheli) for this.
evidence.editorInference: Editor: a secondary paraphrase of a study not in hand; the primary (Vidale & Micheli) is blocked and should replace this record when retrieved.
limitations: Secondary paraphrase of an unretrieved paper.

evidence.title: Deep Memory's caption on the site names of Göbekli Tepe
evidence.sourceStatement: The caption 'Navel hill' states: "The Turkish name describes the mound's shape; the Kurdish names" mean 'wish hill.'
evidence.editorInference: Editor: an unsourced secondary statement; the toponymy needs a primary (excavation reports or a Kurdish/Turkish toponymic source) before it weighs on the navel theme.
limitations: No source given on the page for the etymologies.

claims.statement: Bird-headed figures, handled shapes and hands-resting-on-the-body poses recur on objects from cultures separated by great distance and time (Göbekli Tepe, Nimrud, La Venta, Rapa Nui). True if securely identified objects from each of these places show the named features.

sourceAnchor.quote: distant objects can share a surprisingly familiar visual grammar

claims.statement: The historical meaning of a visual resemblance between objects depends on their dates, contexts, differences and possible connections, not on the resemblance alone. True if no resemblance can be assigned a historical explanation without those data.

sourceAnchor.quote: Its historical meaning depends on the objects' dates, contexts, differences and possible connections.

claims.statement: Olmec Monument 19 from La Venta is the earliest known depiction of a feathered serpent. True if no securely dated feathered-serpent image predates it.

sourceAnchor.quote: Olmec Monument 19, the earliest known feathered serpent.

claims.statement: The description 'bird-man' groups at least three distinct ideas — a deity with a bird's head, a person wearing feathers, and a person transforming into a bird. True if the compared images fall into different ones of these categories.

sourceAnchor.quote: a deity with a bird's head, a person wearing feathers and a person transforming into a bird need not be the same idea

claims.statement: In the Deep Memory catalogue experiment, a broad bird-person motif class occurs in 55% of 926 sampled traditions. True if the experiment's coded data reproduce that proportion.

sourceAnchor.quote: finds its broad bird-person class in 55% of the 926 sampled traditions

claims.statement: A relational comparison of a profile head, a bent or extended limb, and a rounded form nearby is more specific than noting a bird in both pictures. True if the co-occurrence of those three features is rarer across a control set than the presence of a bird.

sourceAnchor.locator: [§ The bird, the bent limb and the circle]
sourceAnchor.quote: a profile head, a bent or extended limb, and a rounded form nearby

claims.statement: The top register of Pillar 43 at Göbekli Tepe carries three arched handled forms with small animals. True if the excavators' record of the pillar shows them.

sourceAnchor.quote: Three arched objects with small animals; function unknown.

claims.statement: The Assyrian banduddû is a bucket named in ritual texts, carried with a cone used to sprinkle from it. True if cuneiform ritual texts name the bucket and describe sprinkling with the cone.

sourceAnchor.quote: A bucket, named in ritual texts, with the cone used to sprinkle from it.

claims.statement: The Jiroft chlorite 'handbag' in the National Museum of Iran shows wear on its handle consistent with having hung on a cord. True if the published wear-trace study reports handle wear of that kind.

sourceAnchor.quote: Worn on the handle as if hung on a cord.

claims.statement: The small handled object held by the seated figure on La Venta Monument 19 is usually read by specialists as an incense bag. True if the standard Olmec literature gives that reading.

sourceAnchor.quote: The seated figure's pouch, usually read as an incense bag.

claims.statement: A handle is a practical solution that can recur independently in unconnected cultures. True if handled containers appear in cultures with no demonstrable contact.

sourceAnchor.quote: A handle is also a practical solution that can recur independently.

claims.statement: The function of the three handled forms on Pillar 43 is uncertain. True if the excavation team has published no secure functional identification.

sourceAnchor.quote: the function of the Göbekli forms remains uncertain

claims.statement: The Göbekli Tepe excavation team's discussion of Enclosure C distinguishes boar sculptures from snarling predators and considers their arrangement at the entrance together. True if the team's publication makes that distinction.

sourceAnchor.locator: [§ Reptile-like forms—and the animal in its setting]
sourceAnchor.quote: distinguishes boars from snarling predators and considers their arrangement together

claims.statement: Shared animal anatomy and carving choices can each contribute to the visual resemblance between pig or boar sculptures from distant cultures. True if a control set of securely identified pig sculptures shares the low body, raised back and projecting snout regardless of culture.

sourceAnchor.locator: [§ Pigs, boars and a compact stone silhouette]
sourceAnchor.quote: Both anatomy and carving choices could contribute

claims.statement: The modern Turkish name Göbekli Tepe ('navel hill') describes the shape of the mound. True if the toponym is documented as descriptive of the mound's form rather than as a sacred designation.

sourceAnchor.quote: The Turkish name describes the mound's shape

claims.statement: The Kurdish names for the Göbekli Tepe site mean 'wish hill'. True if a Kurdish toponymic or ethnographic source records that meaning.

sourceAnchor.quote: the Kurdish names mean "wish hill."

claims.statement: The netted omphalos stone at Delphi marked the sanctuary as the meeting point of Zeus's eagles. True if ancient Greek sources describe the Delphic omphalos in those terms.

sourceAnchor.quote: Netted stone marking the meeting point of Zeus's eagles.

claims.statement: The Greek omphalos, Garcilaso's gloss of Cusco, the Rapanui Te Pito o te Henua and the modern Turkish name Göbekli Tepe are different kinds of evidence, differing in language, date of first record and whether the ancient builders used the name. True if their source histories differ on those three points.

also.quote: what does the expression mean in its language, when is that meaning first recorded, and was it a name the ancient builders used?

claims.statement: The Rapanui name Te Pito Kura means 'navel of light'. True if Rapanui lexical sources give that gloss.

sourceAnchor.quote: Te Pito Kura, "navel of light" Rapa Nui.

claims.statement: Carving limbs against a stone body protects them from breakage, so material constraint is a plausible contributor to the hands-on-body pose of stone figures. True if free-standing carved limbs break more often than limbs carved against the body in comparable stone sculpture.

claims.statement: The fish-cloaked apkallu is the sage type named in Assyrian cuneiform texts, and Berossus's Oannes recalls it. True if the texts name fish-cloaked sages as apkallu and Berossus's description of Oannes matches that type.

sourceAnchor.quote: A colonial recording date is a reason to examine mediation, not proof that every detail was invented by a chronicler.

claims.statement: In the Deep Memory flood text-coding pilot, the coded details of 263 flood-story summaries cluster by region. True if the pilot's coded data show regional clustering under its stated measure.

sourceAnchor.quote: The coded summaries show regional clustering

also.quote: The flood experiment maps details in 263 summaries.

claims.statement: In the same pilot, details associated with Genesis are unevenly distributed across the coded flood summaries while generic flood motifs are widespread. True if the coded data show that contrast.

sourceAnchor.quote: an uneven distribution of details associated with Genesis, alongside widespread generic flood motifs

claims.statement: A proposed connection between distant motifs is more informative when there are dated intermediates, a plausible route, or distinctive details that occur together and predict further evidence. True if cases with those features have historically been confirmed more often than cases without them.

sourceAnchor.quote: dated intermediates, a plausible route, or distinctive details that occur together and predict further evidence

claims.statement: Stories can become more alike than their originals through translation, borrowing and comparative writing. True if documented retellings show convergence of detail relative to earlier attested versions.

sourceAnchor.quote: Stories can also become more alike through translation, borrowing and comparative writing.

claims.statement: Similarity between motifs alone cannot establish a lost-civilisation account's claims about the source's identity, date and capabilities. True if those claims require evidence beyond resemblance.

claims.statement: A visual resemblance between signs of two undeciphered scripts does not establish shared sound, meaning or descent. True if sign-shape similarity can arise between scripts known to be unrelated.

sourceAnchor.quote: A visual resemblance does not establish shared sound, meaning or descent.

claims.statement: In the Deep Memory image pilots, AI judges disagreed strongly with one another about the resemblance between the same objects. True if the pilots' inter-judge agreement statistics are low.

sourceAnchor.quote: unreliable feature coding and strong disagreement between judges

claims.statement: In the Deep Memory catalogue experiment, the three broad motif classes (birds, serpents, sacred centres) are each widespread and their co-occurrence does not stand out against documentation-preserving comparisons. research.title: Retrieve the primary literature the page leans on for the handled objects
research.summary: Obtain the Vidale & Micheli wear-trace study (Iranian Journal of Archaeological Studies), the Tepe Telegrams posts on Pillar 43 (Notroff et al. 2016, 2017) and Sweatman & Tsikritsis 2017, and read them against CLM-DEEP-007, -009, -012 and -042. Record what each states about the handled forms' shape, wear and function, so that the page's secondary captions can be replaced by primary observations.
research.informationGain: Moves the handled-object claims from a founder's captions to the excavators' and wear analysts' own statements; settles whether the 'hung on a cord' wear reading and 'function unknown' are what the primaries say.

research.title: Source history of the four 'navel' names
research.summary: For omphalos (Delphi), Garcilaso's gloss of Cusco, Te Pito o te Henua / Te Pito Kura and Göbekli Tepe, find the earliest attestation of the 'navel' meaning, the language it is recorded in, and whether the builders' own usage is documented — from primary texts (Pausanias/Pindar for Delphi; Garcilaso de la Vega 1609; early Rapanui lexicons; Turkish/Kurdish toponymic records).
research.informationGain: Tests CLM-DEEP-018 directly: if the four names differ in date and origin as the page proposes, the navel parallel drops to a shared bodily metaphor; if any shares an early, builder-used meaning, that is unexpected and worth reporting.

research.title: Blind human lineup test of the civiliser accounts from original passages
research.summary: Rerun the V1 lineup design with human raters and unrecognisable, source-level passages (Berossus via Polyhistor/Eusebius for Oannes; Sarmiento/Betanzos for Viracocha; Sahagún for Quetzalcoatl; Simón for Bochica), with controls from random hero narratives. Compare the first-rank rate to the 62.5% / 9% figures.
research.informationGain: Distinguishes similarity of the original accounts from similarity manufactured by compressed modern retellings — the page's own stated limitation of V1.
